title: The Wire Only Tells Once
passages:
Wren knelt on the wet deck planks and set the twin spool down between her and Sol. Two reels side by side, one for the descent wire and one for its slack. She threaded the leader through the reader, the box that plays back a diver's recorded wire, clicked the pinch roller shut, and spun the take-up reel by hand. The wire sang a soft, even note as it moved through the head.

"Here," Wren said. She kept her eyes on the reels, not on Sol. "Eleven seconds. Snipped clean. The shears are in my pocket. My hand did it."

Sol stood at the rail, one hand on the bell frame, watching the Kettle's gate where Quill waited with the berth book. The storm bell had started its count, a slow brass toll that shook the Marrow's timbers. Dey lay on the deck mat behind them, gray around the mouth, rattling with every breath.

"Show me," Sol said.

Wren fed the wire forward. The reader clicked. A span passed the head, then stopped on a clean cut, both ends blunt and shiny, no fray. Eleven seconds of nothing between them. She stopped the reel.

"Fifty-two minutes," Wren said. "That's what the cut was built to hide. I don't remember any of it. Not the descent, not the can going over the side, not why I'd cut my own wire."

The spit can was the hard-shell drop-box a diver jettisons so the crew gets their record if they don't surface. Its beacon was still transmitting at forty-two meters on six hours of battery. Wren had found it missing from her harness clip earlier, still pinging from depth.

Sol didn't move from the rail. Her face was calm, which was worse than shouting. "The rule on this boat is slates run, nobody cuts, nobody goes down alone."

"I know," Wren said. "I broke all three."

"You went down alone."

"I don't remember going down at all."

"That doesn't make it better." Sol stepped closer, her boots loud on the wet planks. "Hand me the shears."

Wren pulled them from her pocket and dropped them into Sol's palm. Sol closed her fingers around them. They were heavy, rust-spotted at the joint, the kind of tool that could cut a diver's line or a wire span with one squeeze. Eleven seconds of nothing sat on the reader between two clean cuts, and Sol's fist was closed around the shears.

Sol turned the shears over in her palm. The blades caught the gray light coming through the Kettle's gate. She didn't speak.

"Say it," Sol said at last.

Wren wiped her hands on her trousers, leaving a smear of wire grease. "The wire only tells once. You cut a span out, that stretch of record is gone for good. No backup, no second copy, nothing to patch it with. You play a span through the reader, it runs from the master spool onto the take-up reel and it's spent. You can't rewind it, you can't run it back, and you can't thread the same length twice. The record tells its story one time, and then it's silent."

She pointed at the master spool, the larger reel on the left side of the twin spool, where the full descent wire lay wound in overlapping loops. "There's one snipped length still on the master. A second cut. I found it when I wound the wire back after your last run. I haven't threaded it. I haven't dared."

Sol didn't lower her hand. "How long?"

"Eleven seconds. Or less. It's a blind span—no leader, no slack on the take-up side, just wire between two fresh cuts. My cuts. I made them and then I left them sitting there."

"That's not eleven seconds of nothing," Sol said. "That's eleven seconds of something you don't want to hear."

"I don't know what's on it."

"You know well enough."

Dey coughed from the mat, a wet, racking sound that shook his shoulders. He didn't open his eyes. "Get on with it," he muttered. "Before the bell drowns us all."

Wren kicked his boot, light but sharp. "Sleep it off, diver. You're not the one holding the shears."

Dey made a noise that might have been a laugh. "Cut it already. Whatever she did, it's already done."

Sol looked at Wren, not at the wire. "You're afraid of your own record."

"I'm afraid of what happens after I play it," Wren said. "Once it's spent, it's gone. That's the rule. I cut it, so it's mine to play—or not."

Sol's fingers tightened on the shears until the rust-spotted joint creaked. "Then play it."

"I haven't decided if I want to hear my own voice tell me what I did."

Outside, the storm bell tolled again, low and slow, shaking the Marrow's timbers. The reader clicked as the take-up reel settled, a small mechanical sound in the quiet. The unplayed span waited on the master, eleven seconds of wire that had been cut out of Wren's own record, still unspent, still unheard, and still hers.

Sol’s thumb rode the spine of the shears, not opening them, not closing them. She looked at the reader, then at Wren, then at Dey’s chest rising shallow on the mat.

“I’ve got gaps too,” Sol said. “Hours I can’t account for. Maybe days. I never knew how many because I never kept a slate worth reading. I’ve been shading them from the crew, shading them from myself, acting like the helm was mine because I remembered enough to fake it.”

She turned the shears over once, blades catching the gray light from the Kettle’s gate.

“That stops now. Until the channel shuts, the rule on this boat is slates run, nobody cuts, nobody goes down alone. You cut a span, it’s gone. You go down without a tether and a tender, you don’t go down. No exceptions for the captain. No exceptions for the reader. That includes you.”

Wren opened her mouth, but Sol held up the shears.

“Say it. All of it. And mean it, because I’m not asking you to swear on a bible. I’m asking you to swear on the wire, which doesn’t care if you’re sorry.”

Wren looked at the rust-spotted blades. Her throat was dry.

“Slates run,” Wren said. “Nobody cuts. Nobody goes down alone.”

“Again. Louder.”

“Slates run. Nobody cuts. Nobody goes down alone.”

Sol nodded once. She stepped forward and dropped the shears into Wren’s palm. The metal was cold, the joint stiff with rust.

“Keep them on your person,” Sol said. “If I find you with the wire in the reader alone, I’ll lock you in the head and give the helm to Dey.”

Dey coughed from the mat. “I can’t dive. I can still steer.”

“Exactly.”

Sol looked down at Wren. “Fetch Nia. I want that rule in the paper log before the bell counts down to twenty. No slates. No edits. Paper and ink. And then you play the span. All eleven seconds.”

The Kettle’s gate horn sounded once outside, low and impatient. Quill was coming back with the berth book and the indenture and forty minutes that were already half spent.

Wren stood, the shears heavy in her palm. She set her thumb on the take-up reel. The wire gave one soft, even hum, as if something had just touched it from the other side.

Wren left the spool humming and went down the aft hatch into the bunkroom, where the air was warm and smelled of diesel and wet wool. Nia was kneeling at the cold-box with the lid up, thumb-and-forefinger on each vial in the rack, counting by feel because the light down here was a single caged bulb and the bulb was failing.

"Sixteen," Nia said, not looking up. "Fifteen and a stub. Teo's got nine days if he doesn't get sick, four if he does."

"Sol wants the rule in the log."

"Then say it and stop breathing on my vials."

"Slates run. Nobody cuts. Nobody goes down alone."

Nia took the log from under the bunk frame, a hard-backed book with Mercy General stamped on the cover in flaking gold, and licked the carpenter's pencil. She wrote slowly, the way people write who taught themselves late and don't trust their letters. "Again. Slower. I'm not doing your handwriting for you."

Wren said it again, slower. Behind Nia, Teo lay in the bunk with his knees up and his heels drumming the bulkhead, which meant he felt well enough to be a nuisance.

Nia read it back line by line, pencil under each one. "*Slates run.*" She looked up. "That means the recorder stays on. Even when it's ugly. Even when it's you."

"Nobody cuts."

"*Nobody cuts.* Nobody cuts anything, or nobody cuts a span?"

"Nobody cuts a span. And nobody cuts a line. Both."

"Then write both, I'm not your lawyer." Nia wrote both. Then she ruled a line under it, dated it with the tide, and wrote at the bottom: *signed Wren Achebe, who cut.* She turned the book around.

Wren looked at her own name sitting there under six other names, all of them pressed hard enough to dent the page. "You didn't have to put that part."

"I put down what happened. That's the whole point of paper. Your wire's got a hole in it and a warden upstairs owns a book I can't get a pencil into. This one's mine." Nia tapped the cover. "Sign it or don't, but don't stand there like the page's going to bite."

Wren signed it. Her hand was steady enough to annoy her.

Above them, through the hatch, Dey's voice came thin and shredded: "Sign it twice, reader. Once for the one you cut yesterday."

"Go to sleep, Dey."

"I'm gray, not deaf."

Teo stopped drumming his heels. He rolled onto his back and looked at the deckhead, at the water stain shaped like a hand that had been there since the cold-case came up.

"Nia," he said. "What happens to a name that's already promised to the berth book?"

The cold-box lid stayed up. Nia didn't move toward it, which for her was practically shouting.

"Nobody's promised," Wren said.

"The man in the book upstairs. The warden reads it out loud every time the bell goes. Six crates and a name. Whose name do you think, mine? I'm six." He said it flatly, no self-pity, the way kids say arithmetic. "It's Dey's. He's already spent. So if his name's in the book, what happens to it when he stops being able to work? Does it come back out? Or does the book just keep it?"

Wren opened her mouth. Nothing that came to mind was true, and she'd promised herself she was done handing out the comfortable version.

Nia picked up the pencil. She wrote in the margin beside the rule, small and square: *Teo asks what happens to a promised name. Nobody answered.* Then she blew the graphite dust off and closed the book on her thumb to keep the place.

"You could answer him," she said.

"I don't know what happens."

"Then say that. He hates being handled more than he hates bad news." Nia set the book down. "He got handled for a year in a box. So did I."

Teo said, "See. She'd have told you."

"Go to sleep, Teo."

"You go to sleep."

Wren put her hand on the hatch ladder and got two rungs up before the deck changed. Footsteps crossed overhead, unhurried, and the Marrow took somebody's weight on the low side by the gate. The gate horn went again, twice, close enough to rattle the caged bulb.

Boots on the gunwale. A hand came over the rail, ink-stained to the second knuckle, and set the berth book down on the deck with the small flat slap of a thing that has never once been wrong.

"Reader," Quill called down the hatch. "Bring the diver who's for sale."

PASSAGE ENDS

Wren climbed the aft ladder, the signed log tucked under her arm, and stepped onto the wet deck. The shears were still in her pocket, cold against her thigh.

Quill hadn't moved from the gunwale. The berth book lay open beside her. Ink stained her fingers to the second knuckle. The storm bell tolled again, a slow brass shake that made the Marrow's timbers groan.

"The diver," Quill said. "Bring him up."

"He's not cargo," Sol said.

"He's indentured." Quill looked at Dey on the mat, gray around the mouth, rattling with each breath. "The Kettle clinic has a lung rig. They can pump the salt water out of his lungs before it sets. Free of charge."

Dey didn't open his eyes. "Free? That word doesn't exist on your gate."

"It does today," Quill said. "And because I cannot lie, I'll tell you what it costs. You sign yourself bond to the Kettle before the channel shuts. Your name goes into the berth book and stays there until the Factor's collectors say it comes out. You work dock-debt until it's paid, which it won't be, because it compounds at the gate rate. You sleep where they assign you. You breathe air they rent you. That's the whole price."

She tapped the page. "Six crates and an indenture. That's what six berths above waterline cost. You're the indenture. Sign, and your lungs get cleared. Don't sign, and you keep rattling until you stop."

Wren set her jaw. "You don't get to trade him."

"I'm not trading him." Quill's voice was flat. "I'm offering him a choice. He's gray, captain. He's been gray since he surfaced. Without the lavage, his lungs fill and he drowns dry in his own bunk. With it, he lives — and belongs to the Kettle until they say otherwise. Those are the only true figures I have."

Dey opened his eyes. They were bloodshot and tired. "Lavage," he said. "That's the pump that washes salt out of alveoli, isn't it?"

"The clinic calls it a lung rig." Quill didn't flinch. "Same thing. It costs nothing but your name."

Sol stepped between Quill and the mat. "He's not signing anything."

"Then he stays gray," Quill said. "The bell's counting down. Forty minutes were forty minutes ago. Now you've got twenty, maybe less. The beacon at forty-two meters just spent another one."

Outside, the Kettle's gate horn sounded, low and impatient. Quill closed the berth book with a slap and set it on the gunwale, then reached into her coat and drew out a stylus.

"Reader," she said to Wren. "Tell him what happens to a name already promised."

Wren opened her mouth. Nothing came.

Quill laid the stylus on the deck by Dey's hand. "Sign or don't. The tide's going out either way."

"Out of my light, captain."

Sol didn't move. "Dey—"

"You've said it twice already and it got worse both times." Dey got an elbow under himself and pushed up against the mast step, which cost him. The rattle in his chest climbed a gear and he sat with his mouth open until it eased, gray to the lips. "You're standing between me and the pen. You're not the one breathing through a straw."

"I'm not letting them buy you."

"Nobody's buying me. I'm selling. There's a difference and it's mostly who holds the pen." He turned his head enough to see Quill's boots. "Read me the bad half again, warden. Slowly. I like hearing you do it."

Quill didn't soften it. "Indenture means the Kettle owns the hours you're awake. You work the dock-debt at gate rate, and the rate compounds weekly, so the number goes up faster than you can cut it. You sleep where you're assigned. The air you breathe below the low gate is metered and billed. When you're too old to lift, the debt stays and your name stays with it."

"There. That wasn't so hard."

Wren crouched by the mat with the log under her arm. "Put mine in instead. I'm topside, I've got hands, I can work a gate."

"The clinic wants a diver with a year of deep time in him," Quill said. "Not a reader with holes in her week. You'd be no use to them and I'd be one short in my book."

"Charming," Wren said.

"It's true. I don't have another setting."

Sol crouched too, and Dey watched her come with real irritation. "We raised twelve crates of medicine this morning. Six of them buy the berths. There's nothing left over to buy you back."

"I can count, captain. I've been lying here doing it." He nodded at the stylus on the planks. "Twenty minutes ago I was going to dive the tower again with borrowed lungs and buy my freedom off the Factor. That's not a plan, that's a way to end up in an air pocket for fourteen months waiting on a girl who cuts her own wire. This is worse and it's certain. I'll take certain."

"It's not certain. It's a page in her book."

"Everything's a page in somebody's book." He stretched, slow, past Sol's arm, and got two fingers on the brass barrel of the stylus. "Move, captain. You're in my light again."

She moved.

Quill opened the berth book flat on the gunwale. The pages were leather, oil-tanned and thin as a glove, because paper rots in this air and wire can be cut; leather takes a hot point and keeps what it's told. She pressed the stylus to the first line and drew it down, and the smell came up, burnt hide and salt.

Dey watched his name go into the leather in letters that would outlive him.

"Now the other thing," he said. "Put down that I said it myself. Out loud. Not that I was carried."

"The book holds the price," Quill said. "Not the reason."

"Then say the reason where the bell can hear it. That's your whole trouble, isn't it. You can't shade a figure."

Quill straightened. She said it flatly, at full volume, to the gate and the water and the two hundred people on the low dock pretending not to listen: "Dey Okafor agreed with his own mouth, sitting up, unforced, at nineteen minutes to the shut. The lavage is free. The name is not."

Wren knelt and wrote it in Nia's log under the rule, in her own hand, and dated it with the tide. *Dey Okafor said yes himself.* She left the rest of the line blank.

"When do I get pumped?"

"The rig's on the power barge at the east mole. It's a pump, a heater, and a filter the size of a dog, and it does not travel light. The barge is committed there until the bell hits ten." Quill shut the book on her thumb. "You'll be under way by then."

Dey laughed, and the laugh turned into four hard coughs, and he spat something gray onto the deck and looked at it with professional interest. "So I'm bought and not yet fixed. Best of both worlds."

The storm bell tolled, and the Marrow's timbers took it and gave it back. Quill turned her wrist over. There was a slate strapped there, scuffed at the corners, and the numbers on it belonged to a hard-shell can lying in the dark at forty-two meters with its beacon running.

"It just spent another minute," she said. "It has five hours of battery. It does not have five hours, because you have nineteen minutes."

PASSAGE END
